intended_object: The canonical R-linear isomorphism Map(G, M) ≅ M ⊗_R R[G] for a finite index set G. It sends f to ∑_s f(s) ⊗ δ_s, and its inverse sends m ⊗ p to t ↦ p(t)·m. This is read off the docstring, the module documentation and the API lemmas that follow it.
explanation:
The definition chains three Mathlib equivalences: M ⊗ R[G] ≅ M ⊗ (G →₀ R) (via `coeffLinearEquiv`), then ≅ (G →₀ M) (via `finsuppScalarRight`), then ≅ (G → M) (via `linearEquivFunOnFinite`). It takes the inverse of the whole chain. The lemmas proved in the same file confirm that this is the standard map:
- the inverse sends m ⊗ p to t ↦ p.coeff t • m;
- the forward map sends Pi.single s m to m ⊗ single s 1, so f goes to ∑_s f s ⊗ single s 1.

The generality is natural:
- R is any commutative semiring.
- M is any R-module.
- G is any `Finite` type with no group structure required; `R[G]` as a module does not need one.

Finiteness is genuinely needed. G → M agrees with the finitely supported functions only when G is finite, and the module documentation notes this limitation. Mathlib has no single declaration giving this exact equivalence; it supplies only the pieces combined here. There are no degenerate-case problems: for empty G both sides are zero.

This is an explicit canonical isomorphism, used later to transport the twisted action to the diagonal action, so it counts as a mathematical object, and it is formalized correctly.
